exercises.prompt: In this philosophy, what does “Existence exists” rule in?

feedback.quote: Existence exists—and the act of grasping that statement implies two corollary axioms: that something exists which one perceives and that one exists possessing consciousness, consciousness being the faculty of perceiving that which exists.
feedback.note: The sentence starts from the fact that something is, and then names what grasping that fact already uses.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, Galt's Speech, For the New Intellectual, 124

choices.text: There is something. Reality is.
Only ideas exist
Existence is a linguistic convention
Reality exists only while it is perceived

feedback.quote: Existence exists—Consciousness is conscious—A is A.
feedback.note: The first formula is two words: Existence exists.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "Axiomatic Concepts," Introduction to Objectivist Epistemology, 55

exercises.prompt: What does the act of grasping “Existence exists” already imply?

choices.text: Something exists which one perceives, and one exists possessing consciousness
Nothing is real until a wish selects it
Only the act of grasping exists; the something does not
Consciousness comes first and produces existence afterward

feedback.quote: Existence exists—and the act of grasping that statement implies two corollary axioms: that something exists which one perceives and that one exists possessing consciousness, consciousness being the faculty of perceiving that which exists.
feedback.note: To grasp that something is, you are already a conscious being perceiving something that exists. A wish is not what makes that fact true.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, Galt's Speech, For the New Intellectual, 124

exercises.prompt: What does Rand say about a consciousness with nothing to be conscious of?

feedback.quote: A consciousness with nothing to be conscious of is a contradiction in terms.
feedback.note: Awareness with no object is not a special case of awareness. The concept cancels itself.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, Galt's Speech, For the New Intellectual, 124

choices.text: It is a contradiction in terms
It is the primary axiom
It is the goal of knowledge
It is a higher form of awareness

exercises.prompt: Peikoff calls existence which of these?

feedback.note: He adds that there is nothing antecedent to existence and no alternative to it. That further sentence is his, in the same essay. The line above is the one to hold.
feedback.citation: Leonard Peikoff, "The Analytic-Synthetic Dichotomy," Introduction to Objectivist Epistemology, 109

choices.text: A self-sufficient primary
A product of a supernatural dimension
A convention of language
An attribute added to things later

exercises.prompt: Match the item to the description used in these texts.

feedback.note: Three different lines are being matched, so this banner is a paraphrase rather than one quotation. Peikoff calls existence a self-sufficient primary. Galt calls consciousness the faculty of perceiving that which exists. Rand calls identity a corollary of existence. Each of those wordings is quoted on its own floor.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "Axiomatic Concepts," Introduction to Objectivist Epistemology, 55

pairs.right: The faculty of perceiving that which exists

feedback.note: Nothing in that sentence makes existence a product of something prior.
feedback.citation: Leonard Peikoff, "The Analytic-Synthetic Dichotomy," Introduction to Objectivist Epistemology, 109

exercises.prompt: Why does this philosophy refuse the demand to prove that existence exists from outside existence?

feedback.note: Galt’s answer is that the demand asks you to prove existence by means of non-existence, and consciousness by means of unconsciousness. The wording here is ours. His statement of what an axiom is, and of the two corollaries, is quoted in the other questions of this floor.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, Galt's Speech, For the New Intellectual, 155

choices.text: Any proof already uses something that exists and a consciousness aware of it
Textbooks forbid the proof
Only mystics are allowed to prove axioms
Existence is a useful fiction

exercises.prompt: In the one-foot summary, which plain-language line does she attach to metaphysics?

feedback.quote:
1. "Nature, to be commanded, must be obeyed" or "Wishing won't make it so."
2. "You can't eat your cake and have it, too."
3. "Man is an end in himself."
4. "Give me liberty or give me death."
feedback.note: She also offers Francis Bacon’s “Nature, to be commanded, must be obeyed” for the same branch. Item 2 is her plain language for epistemology, item 3 for ethics, item 4 for politics. The Bacon and Henry lines are familiar sayings she uses, not sentences she originated.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "Introducing Objectivism," The Objectivist Newsletter, August 1962, 35

choices.text: Wishing won't make it so.
Man is an end in himself.
Give me liberty or give me death.
You can't eat your cake and have it, too.

exercises.prompt: “Reality exists as an objective absolute” means facts are independent of what?

feedback.quote: Reality exists as an objective absolute—facts are facts, independent of man's feelings, wishes, hopes or fears.
feedback.note: That is her first numbered statement of Objectivism in the same essay as the one-foot list.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "Introducing Objectivism," The Objectivist Newsletter, August 1962, 35

choices.text: Man's feelings, wishes, hopes or fears
The law of identity
